title: Zendrop Pricing Explained: What You Actually Pay in Year One
excerpt: A full-year cost breakdown for dropshipping: plan tiers, per-order product cost, shipping, ad spend, refunds, and the app fees that quietly eat contribution margin.
body: Most pricing pages show a monthly plan and stop there, but a dropshipping store pays six separate bills in its first year: the platform plan, the product cost per order, shipping, advertising, refunds and chargebacks, and the app stack you bolt on to make the whole thing run. If you model only the plan, you will price your products wrong and discover the gap in month three. This walkthrough breaks each line down so you can build a budget that survives contact with real orders.

The platform plan is the easiest line and the least important one. Whether you pay monthly or annually, the subscription is usually a rounding error next to ad spend once you are past a few dozen orders a month. Treat it as fixed overhead and move on. The real variable is what you pay per unit, because that number moves with your supplier, your product mix, and how often you switch catalogs while hunting for a winning product.

Product cost plus shipping is your true cost of goods. Pull the landed number for your top ten SKUs, including the shipping method you actually promise at checkout, and refresh it monthly. Carriers reprice, suppliers adjust, and a product that earned a healthy margin in spring can quietly turn marginal by autumn. Many new stores lose money not on bad products but on stale cost data that never made it back into their pricing sheet.

Advertising is where year-one budgets actually break. A testing phase with no contribution margin is normal and should be capped in advance rather than discovered later. Set a fixed test budget per product, define the conversion rate and average order value a product must hit to graduate, and kill everything else. The goal is to move from paid acquisition toward repeat purchase as fast as your catalog allows, because paid traffic never gets cheaper on its own.

Refunds and chargebacks are the line nobody budgets. On a typical general store a few percent of orders come back as disputes, damaged parcels, or not-as-described claims. Each one costs you the outbound shipping, often the product, and sometimes a fee. Track this as a percentage of revenue from day one. When it climbs above a few percent, the fix is usually supplier quality or listing accuracy rather than better customer service scripts.

Finally, add the app stack. Reviews, email, upsell, and tracking apps each take a small monthly bite, and together they can rival your platform plan. Audit them quarterly and cancel duplicates. Once all six lines sit in one sheet you can finally answer the only question that matters: what does an average order actually contribute after everything is paid. The DTCwise Dropshipping category at /category/dropshipping keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing, and the Zendrop listing at /tool/zendrop shows where it fits.
